Patient Vignette: Margaret

Margaret is a 78-year-old woman, a retired public defender who still consults part-time for a legal aid clinic. She has been married to her husband, Thomas, for fifty-two years. She presents as articulate and sharp, with a dry wit that occasionally surfaces, though it is often undercut by a visible tension in her shoulders and a tendency to startle at the sound of the office door closing.

The event that changed things happened eighteen months ago, in the parking lot of the courthouse where she had worked for decades. It was late, after a long case review. She was walking to her car, keys in hand, when a man she had cross-examined years prior approached her. He was disheveled and angry, muttering about a conviction he believed she had orchestrated. Before she could respond, he struck her across the face with a closed fist, then shoved her to the ground. He did not take her purse. He did not say much else. He simply walked away. She lay on the asphalt for what felt like an eternity, staring at the undercarriage of a parked SUV, until a security guard found her.

Physically, she healed. A cracked rib, a bruised orbit, stitches above her left eyebrow. The scar is now a faint white line. But the world has not felt safe since that night.

Margaret describes a constant, low-grade vigilance that she calls "the hum." It is the feeling of being watched, of knowing that a threat could materialize from any direction. She no longer walks to her car alone. Thomas drives her to the clinic and picks her up, waiting at the curb with the engine running. She has stopped going to the grocery store, the pharmacy, the post office. Her life has contracted to the path between her home office and the kitchen table.

She struggles with sleep. She will drift off, only to jerk awake an hour later, her heart pounding, convinced she heard footsteps in the hallway. She has started sleeping in the guest room because she cannot bear the sensation of being exposed in the dark. Thomas, she says, is patient, but she sees the worry in his eyes, and it makes her feel like a burden.

The most difficult part for Margaret is the memory. It is not a narrative she can tell; it is a sensory ambush. A sudden shadow on the wall will bring back the cold feel of the asphalt against her cheek. The sound of a car door slamming in the parking lot will make her flinch, and for a moment, she is back on the ground, waiting for the next blow. She cannot look at her own reflection in a dark window without seeing the man's face.

Her work has suffered. She used to be a formidable advocate, her mind a steel trap for legal precedent. Now, she finds it hard to concentrate. She will be reading a brief and her eyes will slide off the page, her thoughts looping back to the parking lot. She has turned down two new cases, telling her colleagues she is "slowing down," but the truth is she cannot stomach the thought of being in a courtroom, of standing in front of a judge, of being exposed and vulnerable.

She sometimes wonders if she is becoming paranoid. She checks the locks on the doors three times before bed. She has a small can of pepper spray in her purse, in her desk drawer, and on the nightstand in the guest room. She knows it is irrational. The man was arrested the next day. He is in prison. But the feeling does not respond to logic. It lives in her body, a permanent knot in her stomach.

What Margaret does not say, but what is evident in the way she holds herself, is a profound sense of shame. She spent her entire career defending others, believing in the power of the law to provide safety and order. Now, she feels that the world she believed in has been shattered. She is not the person she was. She is a woman who is afraid of the dark, afraid of a parking lot, afraid of a sound. She is, for the first time in her long life, a victim, and she cannot find her way back to being anything else.
